title: Scaling Up and Out
summary: Know when to buy a bigger machine versus more machines, why horizontal scaling needs stateless servers, and the usual path from one box to a sharded system.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between **vertical** and **horizontal** scaling? Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
keyPoints: Vertical (scale up) = a bigger/more powerful single machine; horizontal (scale out) = more machines sharing the work
Vertical advantage: simple, no code changes, no distributed-systems problems
Vertical disadvantage: hard ceiling on machine size, cost rises steeply at the top, still a single point of failure
Horizontal advantage: near-unlimited growth and fault tolerance (one machine can die)
Horizontal disadvantage: needs a load balancer and shared state, adds operational and distributed complexity

questions.hint: Where does `loginAttempts` live, and how many of them are there now?
keyPoints: The counter is in-process state: each of the 4 servers has its own separate object
With round-robin, an attacker gets about 5 attempts per server, so ~20 total instead of 5; the limit is not enforced
The counts are also lost whenever a server restarts or deploys
Fix: store the counter in a shared store such as Redis using an atomic increment (INCR) with an expiry (EXPIRE)
Mentions this makes the app servers stateless and interchangeable

questions.prompt: Your app has scaled out to 10 web servers. How do you handle **user sessions**? Compare at least two approaches.
questions.hint: Who remembers that this browser is logged in: one server, a shared store, or the browser itself?
keyPoints: Sticky sessions: load balancer pins a user to one server; simple but users lose sessions if that server dies and load can be uneven
Central session store (e.g. Redis): cookie holds a session ID, any server looks it up; servers stay stateless; the store must be fast and highly available
Signed tokens (e.g. JWT): identity carried in the token, no lookup needed; downside is revocation before expiry is hard
Recommends a central store or tokens over sticky sessions as the primary approach

questions.prompt: A startup runs everything (web app and PostgreSQL) on one server. Traffic is growing 3× a year and the CPU is at 85% at peak. Walk through what you'd do over the next couple of years, in order.
questions.hint: Find out which part is the bottleneck first. What's the easiest thing to split off?
keyPoints: First measure which component uses the CPU (app vs database)
Separate the database onto its own machine so each tier can be sized independently
Make the app tier stateless and run several copies behind a load balancer (removes the single point of failure)
Scale the database up first, then add a cache and read replicas for read-heavy traffic
Shard only when writes or data size outgrow one primary, because it adds the most complexity

questions.prompt: You need to serve **24,000 peak QPS**. Option A: big servers that each handle **8,000 QPS** at **$2,000/month** each. Option B: small servers that each handle **1,500 QPS** at **$300/month** each. You must survive **one server failing** at peak. How many of each do you need, and which is cheaper?
questions.hint: Compute the minimum count, then add one spare (N + 1).
keyPoints: A: 24,000 / 8,000 = 3, plus 1 spare = 4 servers, cost 4 × $2,000 = $8,000/month
B: 24,000 / 1,500 = 16, plus 1 spare = 17 servers, cost 17 × $300 = $5,100/month
B is cheaper and losing one small server removes a smaller share of capacity (1/17 vs 1/4)
Mentions the trade-off: more servers means more to operate, but autoscaling is finer-grained
questions.answer: A: `24,000/8,000 = 3`, `+1 = 4` → `$8,000/mo`. B: `24,000/1,500 = 16`, `+1 = 17` → `$5,100/mo`. B is cheaper, and a single failure costs only ~6% of capacity instead of 25%.

questions.prompt: Users upload profile pictures. Today the server saves them to `./uploads/` on its local disk and serves them from there. You're moving to 8 stateless servers with autoscaling. Redesign the upload and serving flow.
questions.hint: Where can every server (and the browser) find the file? Who should actually carry the bytes?
keyPoints: Local disk breaks: a file saved on server A is missing on the others, and autoscaling deletes disks of removed servers
Store files in shared object storage (e.g. S3), and only metadata (user id, object key) in the database
Optionally let the browser upload directly to object storage with a presigned URL so the bytes don't go through the app servers
Serve images through a CDN in front of object storage for speed and lower load
App servers end up stateless: any server can handle any request
